point: The chapter reviews flexibility concepts, then assessments of power-to-gas in renewable systems, using standard academic databases.
Flexibility means balancing load and generation, is not new, but is needed more as renewable variability grows.
Flexibility is grouped into supply side and demand side, described by technical parameters or imposed consumption changes.
Grid extension and interconnection reduce the need for flexibility but meet public opposition.
Studies disagree on whether storage is the best flexibility option, so system boundaries and objectives matter.
System flexibility must grow with renewable share, requiring a mix of storage, curtailment and demand response.
Curtailment signals insufficient flexibility and is therefore used as an indicator of flexibility needs.
Sector coupling provides flexibility mainly on the demand side, so power-to-gas is treated that way here.
Most research on power-to-gas uses techno-economic optimisation models, and representative ones are discussed.
A Dutch MILP finds storage cuts costs most with high wind, yet power-to-gas may not be optimal there.
For Germany at high renewable share, power-to-gas is placed mostly in the north and absorbs surplus electricity.
Optimal power-to-gas scheduling in Denmark modestly reduces system cost and wind curtailment.
Hydrogen injection into the British gas grid substantially reduces wind curtailment, especially on low-demand days.
Many power-to-gas studies are too optimistic by ignoring uncertainty and gas security; including them, power-to-gas still eases congestion.
Power-to-gas combined with CHP lowers cost and smooths demand, trading cost savings against smoothing.
A compensation mechanism lets a joint power-to-gas and gas-fired unit help manage congestion.
A Western Balkan model shows flexible technologies, including pumped hydro, can integrate substantial renewables, more with transmission expansion.
Existing models either capture sequential markets or single-step dispatch, and this thesis adds sequential markets and limited foresight.
Redispatch-based flexibility is under-studied, so the thesis assesses the locational as well as temporal value of power-to-gas.
Model studies assume a benevolent single optimiser and neglect regulation, so the thesis adds a regulatory perspective.
